# Chip

A value the reader has added — a recipient, a selected filter, a tag on a record — shown with a control to remove it.

**Not implemented yet.** This page is the *approved intent* — the props API signed off at gate 1 of the build order, before any React exists. Do not import it; there is nothing to import.

| | |
|---|---|
| Registry name | `chip` |
| Family | inputs |
| Tier | free |
| Status (css / react / figma) | future / future / future |
| Depends on | `state-layer`, `icon` |

## Behavior

A `<span>` holding the value's text and a `<button type="button">` that removes it. No primitive: the only behaviour is one button, and Button's activation already owns it.

- **One component, and it is the input chip — the other four chips are already here** — 'Chip' names five things that share a pill shape and differ in semantics, which is this system's test for splitting. A filter chip is a pressed toggle — a row of them is ToggleButtonGroup with `selectionMode="multiple"` and `attached={false}`, announced with `aria-pressed`. A choice chip is one answer from a few — SegmentedControl, or ToggleButtonGroup in single mode, announced as a radio group. A static tag is a label nobody acts on — Badge. An assist or suggestion chip is an action — a small secondary Button. The one thing left is a value the reader added and can take away, which is text plus a removal command, and no existing component is that. Shipping a `Chip` with a `kind` prop over all five would put a radiogroup, a toggle, a label, a button and a removable value behind one name, and the prop would be choosing the ARIA pattern — exactly the mistake Tabs and SegmentedControl were split to avoid.
- **`onRemove` is required** — A chip that cannot be removed is a Badge. Making the handler optional would make this a second way to draw a static label, and the two would drift; requiring it means reaching for this component is itself the statement that the value is removable.
- **The chip is not focusable — its remove button is** — There is one thing to do with a chip, so there is one tab stop: the button. A focusable chip around a focusable button would be two stops for one action, and a focusable chip with no button would need a keyboard command nobody could discover. The button's name is the full phrase, so focusing it says both what the value is and what will happen.
- **The remove button is named after the value** — Five buttons called 'Remove' tell a screen-reader user nothing about which recipient each one removes. The default name is 'Remove' followed by the chip's text — 'Remove Ada Lovelace' — and `removeLabel` replaces the whole phrase, rather than a prefix, so a translation can put the words in its own order.
- **Backspace and Delete on the focused remove button also remove** — Enter and Space activate it because it is a button. Backspace and Delete are what a reader expects to remove a selected value in every token field they have used, and on native platforms 'delete' is the standard accessibility action for exactly this. Accepting them costs nothing and removes a moment of 'how do I get rid of this'.
- **Focus after removal is the caller's, until a multi-value field exists** — Removing the chip removes the focused button, and a browser whose focused element disappears sends focus to `<body>` — a keyboard user is thrown to the top of the page. This component cannot fix that alone: only something that holds all the chips knows that the next one, or the input they were typed into, is where focus should go. So the obligation is stated on `onRemove`: move focus before or as you remove. The real fix is a multi-value field — a text input with its chips, roving focus between them, and Backspace in an empty input removing the last one — which this system does not have and which needs its own gate 1.
- **Long values truncate, and the full value stays reachable** — An email address can be wider than a phone. The text truncates with an ellipsis at the container's width, which is the one place truncation is acceptable: the full value is still the remove button's name and the chip's `title`, so a screen reader and a long-press both have it. Text's contract declined line clamping in general precisely because truncated text needs that second path, and here it already exists.
- **Touch target: size.target.min** — The hit area is size.target.min, 48px, on every platform — Material's minimum, which also clears Apple's 44pt and WCAG 2.5.5. It sizes where the control can be tapped, never the drawn box. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).
- **Web and native** — On the web it renders `<span>` with the text and `<button type="button" aria-label="Remove …">` holding an `aria-hidden` glyph, with `aria-disabled` on the button when disabled. A set of chips is the caller's `<ul role="list">` with one per `<li>`, so the count is announced. On React Native it renders a `View` with `accessible`, `accessibilityLabel` set to the value, and `accessibilityActions={[{ name: "delete", label: removeLabel }]}` handled by `onAccessibilityAction` — one focus stop with the platform's own delete action, which is the native idiom and the reason the web needs a separate button and native does not. The visible remove `Pressable` is then `importantForAccessibility="no-hide-descendants"` / `accessibilityElementsHidden`, so it is a touch target and not a second stop. `className` is web-only; no prop is native-only. There is no gesture: removal is always a press. Rata-drawn (decision N5): neither platform's OS controls include an input chip, so it is drawn from the same recipe; the delete action is the OS accessibility action. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

## Props

| Prop | Type | Default | Summary |
|---|---|---|---|
| `children` | `string` | — | The value, as text. |
| `onRemove` | `() => void` | — | Called when the reader removes the value — by pressing the button, or by Backspace or Delete while it has focus. |
| `removeLabel?` | `string` | `"Remove " + children` | The remove button's full accessible name. |
| `icon?` | `LucideIcon` | — | A glyph before the text that says what kind of value it is. |
| `disabled?` | `boolean` | — | Blocks removal while keeping the button focusable and announced. |
| `className?` | `string` | — | Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it. |

### `children`

```ts
children: string
```

The value, as text.

**Use when**

- A recipient's name or address, a filter's value, a tag.

**Don't use for**

- Markup. The text is reused in the remove button's name and the `title`, so it is a string rather than a ReactNode.

**Accessibility** Read as plain text, and appended to the remove button's default name.

### `onRemove`

```ts
onRemove: () => void
```

Called when the reader removes the value — by pressing the button, or by Backspace or Delete while it has focus.

**Use when**

- Removing the value from the caller's state, and moving focus in the same handler: to the next chip's remove button, or to the field the chips belong to.

**Don't use for**

- Leaving focus where it was. The focused element is about to be removed, and focus falls to `<body>`.
- Asking for confirmation. Removing a chip is undone by adding the value back; a dialog for that is friction with no safety in it.

**Accessibility** The caller owns where focus goes next — see the decision on focus after removal.

### `removeLabel`

```ts
removeLabel?: string = "Remove " + children
```

The remove button's full accessible name.

**Use when**

- A translated phrase, in whatever word order the language needs: `removeLabel={t("remove", { name })}`.

**Don't use for**

- A bare 'Remove' or '×'. It must name the value, or every chip's button sounds the same.

**Accessibility** Becomes the button's `aria-label`, and on native the label of the `delete` accessibility action.

### `icon`

```ts
icon?: LucideIcon
```

A glyph before the text that says what kind of value it is.

**Use when**

- A mail glyph on an address that is not a known contact, beside chips that are.

**Don't use for**

- The same glyph on every chip in a set. If it does not distinguish anything it is noise.

**Accessibility** Decorative — `aria-hidden`. If the kind of value matters, say it in the text.

### `disabled`

```ts
disabled?: boolean
```

Blocks removal while keeping the button focusable and announced.

**Use when**

- A value the reader cannot remove right now — a required recipient, a filter locked by a permission.

**Don't use for**

- A value that can never be removed. That is a Badge.

**Accessibility** `aria-disabled` on the remove button, not the `disabled` attribute, so it stays in the tab order and is announced as unavailable.

### `className`

```ts
className?: string
```

Extra classes, for placement — not for restyling it.

**Use when**

- Rare. A set of chips gets its gap from the list that holds them.

**Don't use for**

- A status colour to mark an invalid value. Invalid input is a Field's message, and a red chip with no words says only 'something is wrong'.

## Use cases

### Recipients added to a message

A set of values the reader built up and may trim.

```tsx
<ul role="list" aria-label="Recipients">
  {recipients.map((person, i) => (
    <li key={person.id}>
      <Chip onRemove={() => removeRecipient(i)}>{person.name}</Chip>
    </li>
  ))}
</ul>
```

Each button is named 'Remove <name>'. `removeRecipient` must move focus to the next chip's button, or to the To field when the last chip goes — the component cannot, because it does not know what comes after it.

### The active filters above a result list

Filters chosen elsewhere — in a Sheet of options — shown as a summary the reader can clear one by one.

```tsx
<Chip onRemove={() => clearFilter("colour")} removeLabel="Clear colour filter: Blue">Blue</Chip>
```

This is the removable summary of a filter, not the filter control. The control that sets it — a row of toggles — is ToggleButtonGroup with `selectionMode="multiple"`.

### Reaching for the wrong component: a filter toggle

A row of options above a list, each turning a filter on or off in place.

```tsx
<Chip onRemove={() => {}}>Unread</Chip>
```

Don't. A filter that toggles in place is pressed or not pressed, and that is ToggleButtonGroup with `selectionMode="multiple"` and `attached={false}`, which announces `aria-pressed`. An empty `onRemove` is the giveaway — there is nothing to remove.

### Reaching for the wrong component: a status label

A label on a record that says what state it is in.

```tsx
<Chip onRemove={noop}>Paid</Chip>
```

Don't. Nobody removes 'Paid' from an invoice by pressing an ×. That is a Badge, with `variant="success"`.

## Token recipe

### base

An outlined value, drawn with the secondary role so it reads as something the reader can act on rather than as a status. That is the visible difference from a neutral Badge, which is a filled label that nobody removes.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| background | `theme.secondary-role.bg` |
| border | `border.default solid theme.secondary-role.border` |
| color | `theme.secondary-role.fg — verified on theme.secondary-role.bg` |
| block-size | `size.control.sm` |
| padding-inline-start | `space.control.padding-inline.sm` |
| padding-inline-end | `space.1 — the remove control sits in the end padding's place` |
| border-radius | `radius.element — documented as the radius for chips` |
| gap between icon, text and remove control | `space.gap.xs` |
| font-size | `type.control.size.sm` |
| font-weight | `type.label.weight` |
| line-height | `type.control.line-height.sm` |
| leading icon size | `size.icon.text` |
| max-inline-size | `100% of its container, with the text truncated by an ellipsis — the full value stays the remove control's name and the chip's title` |
| disabled | `state.disabled-opacity, on the whole chip` |

### remove

The one interactive part. Visibly small, with a hit area stretched to the chip's full block size and past its end.

| Property | Token |
|---|---|
| visible inline-size / block-size | `size.icon.md` |
| glyph size | `size.icon.sm` |
| glyph colour | `theme.fg.secondary` |
| border-radius | `radius.pill` |
| hit area | `size.target.min in both dimensions, centred on the visible remove circle with a pseudo-element; the circle itself stays small so the chip stays a chip` |
| hover / press | `compose the .rata-state-layer class` |
| focus ring | `theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible` |
